lesson.title: Build a Better ls CLI in Rust with Clap
lesson.goal: build a command-line tool in Rust with cargo that parses arguments

sources.title: Build a Better ls CLI in Rust with Clap

steps.title: Create project and parse args
steps.instructions: Run `cargo new best_ls`, add clap with the derive feature to Cargo.toml, and define `#[derive(Parser)] struct Cli { path: Option<PathBuf> }` with `Cli::parse()` in main. Run `cargo run -- -h` to see the generated help.

targets.caption: clap dependency with the derive feature
Derive Parser on the Cli struct
Parse command-line args in main
Auto-generated help from clap

explanations.topic: clap's derive feature makes argument parsing easy
Taking a path as the first positional argument
Parser derive adds the parse method
Using -- to pass arguments through cargo run
Reading the generated usage/arguments/options help

hints: Add clap to Cargo.toml with features = ["derive"], or run `cargo add clap --features derive`.
Define `struct Cli { path: Option<PathBuf> }` and put `#[derive(Parser)]` above it.
Import with `use clap::Parser;` and `use std::path::PathBuf;`, then call `let cli = Cli::parse();` in main.
Run `cargo run -- -h`; the `--` sends -h to your program instead of cargo.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the "derive" feature, so `#[derive(Parser)]` isn't found.
Not importing `clap::Parser`, so `Cli::parse()` doesn't resolve.
Running `cargo run -h`, which shows cargo's help instead of your app's.
Using `PathBuf` without `use std::path::PathBuf`.
Making path a required `PathBuf` instead of `Option<PathBuf>`, so help shows <PATH> instead of [PATH].

steps.title: Add version, about, default path
steps.instructions: Add `#[command(version, about, long_about = "...")]` to the Cli struct and check `cargo run -- --version`. Default the path with `cli.path.unwrap_or(PathBuf::from("."))` and print `path.display()`, then run `cargo run -- long_path`.

targets.caption: Clap command attribute adds --version and about text
Fall back to current directory when no path is given
Run with and without a path argument

explanations.topic: #[command(version)] auto-generates a --version flag from Cargo.toml
long_about text shows in --help output
cli.path is an Option, so unwrap_or supplies a default
Defaulting to '.' mirrors ls listing the current directory

hints: Add a #[command(...)] attribute right under #[derive(Parser)] on your Cli struct.
Inside it, list version, about, and long_about = "..."; then try cargo run -- --version and cargo run -- --help.
cli.path is Option<PathBuf>: use cli.path.unwrap_or(PathBuf::from(".")).
PathBuf doesn't implement Display, so print it with println!("{}", path.display()).
common_mistakes: Forgetting the `--` in `cargo run -- --version`, so cargo consumes the flag instead of your program.
Printing the PathBuf directly with {} instead of calling .display().
Not importing std::path::PathBuf.
Writing longabout instead of long_about in the attribute.
Putting #[command(...)] above #[derive(Parser)] on a different item or misspelling it as #[clap] with mismatched clap version.

steps.title: Check path existence with colors
steps.instructions: Add owo-colors to Cargo.toml and in src/main.rs use `if let Ok(does_exist) = fs::exists(&path)`, printing "Path does not exist" in red when false and "Error reading directory" in red on Err. Run `cargo run -- somepath` to see the red message.

targets.caption: Check whether the given path exists
owo-colors dependency added
Red message for a missing path

explanations.topic: fs::exists tells you whether a path exists
Adding the owo-colors crate for colored output
cargo build puts the debug executable in target/debug
fs::exists returns Err when existence cannot be confirmed or denied

hints: Add owo-colors under [dependencies] in Cargo.toml, or run `cargo add owo-colors`.
fs::exists(&path) returns a Result<bool>, so use `if let Ok(does_exist) = ...` and add an else branch for the Err case.
Import the trait with `use owo_colors::OwoColorize;` so `"Path does not exist".red()` compiles.
Pass a fake path after `--`: `cargo run -- somepath`.
common_mistakes: Forgetting `use owo_colors::OwoColorize;`, which gives a 'no method named red' error.
Treating fs::exists as returning bool instead of Result<bool>.
Omitting `--` in `cargo run -- somepath`, so the argument goes to cargo instead of your program.
Not handling the Err branch ('Error reading directory').
Leaving the earlier debug print of the path in place, which clutters the output.

steps.title: List directory file names
steps.instructions: In src/main.rs write `fn get_files(path: &Path) -> Vec<String>` that uses `fs::read_dir` and pushes each entry's file name. Loop over `get_files(&path)`, print each name, then run `cargo run`.

targets.caption: New helper that returns the directory's file names
Read the directory entries with fs::read_dir
Files in the current directory printed

explanations.topic: get_files returns Vec<String> for now, to be expanded later
if let Ok(...) over fs::read_dir to handle read errors
file_name().into_string() and unwrap_or fallback
cargo run with no args lists the working directory

hints: Write a function that takes a &Path and returns Vec<String>, starting from an empty vector that you return at the end.
Use `if let Ok(read_dir) = fs::read_dir(path)` and then `for entry in read_dir`, with another `if let Ok(file) = entry`.
Push `file.file_name().into_string().unwrap_or("unknown name".into())` into the vector.
In main, loop `for file in get_files(&path) { println!("{}", file); }` then run `cargo run`.
common_mistakes: Forgetting `use std::fs;` or `use std::path::Path;`, which causes unresolved-name errors.
Passing `path` instead of `&path` to get_files, giving a mismatched-types error.
Declaring the vector without `mut`, so push fails to compile.
Treating into_string() like an Option: it returns Result<String, OsString>, but unwrap_or still works.
Placing the loop outside the branch where the path exists.

steps.title: Collect file metadata into structs
steps.instructions: Add strum (features = ["derive"]) and define `enum EntryType { File, Dir }` plus `struct FileEntry` with name, e_type, len_bytes and modified fields. Fill them from `fs::metadata` in `map_data`, make `get_files` return `Vec<FileEntry>`, and print the result with `{:#?}`.

targets.caption: Struct holding each file's metadata
File or Dir, with strum's Display derive
Helper that turns a DirEntry into a FileEntry
Pretty-printed metadata from {:#?}

explanations.topic: Designing a struct to hold file metadata
Enum for entry type (file vs directory)
Adding strum's Display derive to print enums as strings
Using fs::metadata with if let Ok
Bug: passing the directory path instead of the file's path to metadata
Extracting the logic into a map_data function

hints: Add strum to Cargo.toml with the derive feature (e.g. `cargo add strum --features derive`), then `use strum::Display;`.
Define `FileEntry { name: String, e_type: EntryType, len_bytes: u64, modified: String }` and derive Debug on both it and EntryType so `{:#?}` works.
Inside the loop, use `if let Ok(meta) = fs::metadata(&file.path())`, then pick `EntryType::Dir` when `meta.is_dir()`, else `EntryType::File`, and set `len_bytes: meta.len()`.
Make get_files return `Vec<FileEntry>`, move the push into a `map_data(file, &mut data)` helper, and print with `println!("{:#?}", get_files(&path))`.
common_mistakes: Calling fs::metadata on the directory `path` instead of `file.path()`, so every entry shows the same metadata.
Naming the field `type`, which is a reserved Rust keyword (the presenter uses `e_type`).
Forgetting `#[derive(Debug)]` on FileEntry or EntryType, so `{:#?}` fails to compile.
Adding strum without the `derive` feature, so `strum::Display` can't be found.
Using `{:?}` instead of `{:#?}` and getting one unreadable line instead of pretty-printed output.

steps.title: Render colored table with tabled
steps.instructions: Add the tabled crate, derive `Tabled` on FileEntry (and Display on the enum), build `Table::new(get_files(&path))`, apply `Style::rounded()` and color columns/rows via `table.modify(Columns::first(), Color::FG_BRIGHT_CYAN)` etc. Rename headers with `#[tabled(rename = "Type")]`/`"Size B"` and run `cargo run`.

targets.caption: Build the table from get_files(&path)
Rounded border style
Color columns and header row
Rename column headers
Renamed header in output

explanations.topic: What the tabled crate does: print structs as ASCII tables
Applying a table style (rounded, nushell-like)
Targeting columns/rows with modify to add colors
Renaming headers with #[tabled(rename)]

hints: Add tabled to Cargo.toml dependencies and derive Tabled on FileEntry.
Every field in a Tabled struct must implement Display, so implement fmt::Display for your entry-type enum.
Replace the print loop with `let mut table = Table::new(get_files(&path));` then `println!("{}", table);`.
Use `table.with(Style::rounded())` and `table.modify(Columns::first(), Color::FG_BRIGHT_CYAN)`; import Columns/Rows from tabled::settings::object.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to derive Tabled on FileEntry, so Table::new won't compile
Enum field lacks a Display impl, causing a trait-bound error
Not declaring table as `mut` before calling with/modify
Importing Style/Color from the wrong module (they live under tabled::settings)
Misspelling the color constant (e.g. FG_BRIGHT_MAGNET instead of FG_BRIGHT_MAGENTA)

steps.title: Format modified dates with chrono
steps.instructions: Add chrono and in `map_data` use `if let Ok(modi) = meta.modified()` to convert into `DateTime<Utc>` and set `modified` to `date.format("%a %b %e %Y").to_string()`, else an empty string. Run `cargo run -- src` to see dates in the table.

targets.caption: Convert SystemTime into a chrono DateTime<Utc>
strftime-style format string for the Modified column
Build succeeds and the table prints with dates

explanations.topic: Why chrono: std has no date formatting, only SystemTime
Falling back to an empty string when modified time is unavailable
meta.modified() returns a Result<SystemTime>
Converting SystemTime into DateTime<Utc> with .into()
Format specifiers (%a %b %e %Y) for printing dates

hints: Add chrono to the [dependencies] section of Cargo.toml (or run `cargo add chrono`), then go to the place in map_data where the `modified` field is set.
Call `meta.modified()`. It returns a Result<SystemTime>, so wrap it in `if let Ok(modi) = ... { ... } else { String::default() }`.
Inside the Ok branch, write `let date: DateTime<Utc> = modi.into();`. You also need `use chrono::{DateTime, Utc};` at the top of the file.
Return `date.format("%a %b %e %Y").to_string()` (or wrap it in `format!`), then run `cargo run -- src`.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to add chrono to Cargo.toml, which gives an 'unresolved import chrono' error.
Missing `use chrono::{DateTime, Utc};`, so DateTime or Utc is not found.
Leaving out the type annotation `DateTime<Utc>` on the binding, so `.into()` can't infer its target type.
Naming the binding `mod`. It is a reserved keyword, so use something like `modi`.
Not returning a String from both branches: the else must produce String::default() or String::new(), not "" as &str.
Passing the path without `--`, so cargo swallows the argument.

steps.title: Add --json flag with serde
steps.instructions: In src/main.rs add `#[arg(short, long)] json: bool` to Cli, extract `print_table`, add serde (derive) and serde_json to Cargo.toml, and derive `Serialize` on FileEntry and EntryType. When `cli.json` is set, print `serde_json::to_string(&get_files(&path))`, then test with `cargo run -- -j` and `cargo run -- --help`.

targets.caption: Clap attribute giving the json field -j and --json flags
Branch: print JSON or fall back to print_table
Serialize the file entries to a JSON string
New flag shown in --help

explanations.topic: Without #[arg(short, long)] clap treats the field as positional; the attribute creates -j/--json
Extracting the table printing into a print_table function
serde with derive plus serde_json for serializing data to JSON
Every nested type (the EntryType enum) must also derive Serialize
to_string returns a Result; unwrap_or supplies a fallback string

hints: Add a `json: bool` field to your Cli struct and annotate it so clap creates both a short and long flag.
Run `cargo add serde --features derive` and `cargo add serde_json`, then `use serde::Serialize;`.
Add `Serialize` to the derive list of both FileEntry and EntryType, or the compiler will complain that EntryType doesn't implement Serialize.
In main: `if cli.json { println!("{}", serde_json::to_string(&get_files(&path)).unwrap_or("cannot parse json".to_string())); } else { print_table(path); }`
common_mistakes: Adding `json: bool` without `#[arg(short, long)]`, so clap treats it as a required positional argument instead of a flag.
Forgetting the `derive` feature on serde, so `#[derive(Serialize)]` is not found.
Deriving Serialize on FileEntry but not on the EntryType enum it contains.
Running `cargo run -j` instead of `cargo run -- -j`, which passes -j to cargo rather than your program.
Passing a String to `unwrap_or` incorrectly (e.g. `&str` without `.to_string()`), causing a type mismatch.
